cards.q: What is HTTPS and why is it recommended on Cisco devices?
cards.a: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS on TCP 443 that encrypts web-management sessions; on Cisco devices it is the recommended embedded web server, enabled with a trustpoint/certificate.

cards.q: What does TLS add over plain HTTP?
cards.a: Port 443 instead of 80, TLS record encryption of the payload, server authentication via certificate, and integrity via the TLS MAC/records.

cards.q: What happens in a simplified TLS handshake?
cards.a: The client sends ClientHello, the server replies ServerHello plus its certificate, the client verifies the cert and exchanges keys, then both sides send Finished and the encrypted channel is live.

cards.q: What are the key commands to enable the Cisco secure web server?
cards.a: crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048 for the device keypair, ip http secure-server to enable HTTPS, ip http secure-port 443, ip http authentication local, and ip http access-class to restrict access.

cards.q: What happens if no RSA keypair is generated on the device?
cards.a: The secure (HTTPS) server cannot start, because the RSA keypair is required for the TLS server key exchange.

cards.q: What are the certificate options on Cisco devices?
cards.a: Self-signed certificates are generated locally for labs and quick setups, while CA-signed certificates from a trusted CA are used in production; modern browsers warn on self-signed unless a fingerprint is trusted.

cards.q: How do HTTPS and SSH compare as management protocols?
cards.a: HTTPS provides web GUI/REST access on TCP 443 with local or token authentication, while SSH provides CLI exec sessions on TCP 22; both are encrypted management channels.

cards.q: What are the recommended HTTPS security practices on network devices?
cards.a: Disable plain HTTP to avoid cleartext, apply an ACL to the management port, rotate certificates to maintain trust, and use AAA to centralize authentication.

cards.q: Why would HTTPS fail to load or show TLS errors?
cards.a: A missing RSA key (generate one), self-signed certificate warnings (use a CA trustpoint), TCP 443 blocked (ACL), an authentication loop (AAA config), or time/cert mismatch fixed by NTP plus valid certs.

cards.q: What is the relationship between NTP and certificate validity?
cards.a: A clock mismatch makes certificates appear invalid, so NTP keeps device time correct and avoids certificate-validity issues in TLS.

cards.q: Which command enables HTTPS versus the insecure plain HTTP server?
cards.a: ip http secure-server enables HTTPS, while ip http server is its insecure plain-HTTP twin; HTTPS uses port 443 and HTTP uses port 80.

cards.q: What should be the expected answer for web GUI or REST management of a device?
cards.a: HTTPS (TCP 443), which encrypts management sessions; plain HTTP on 80 is discouraged.
